newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: World wheat prices seen under pressure in 1997-GCA.
newsitem.headline: World wheat prices seen under pressure in 1997-GCA.

text.p: The prospect of another large world wheat harvest in 1997/98 and an increase in world stocks are expected to keep prices under pressure, Grains Council of Australia (GCA) president Jeff Arney said on Tuesday.
The big harvests also increased the prospect of the European Union and the United States renewing their subsidy war, he said.

Arney told the Grains Week 1997 conference that grower confidence would be boosted by the Australian Wheat Board's 1996/97 (June 30) pool price increase for Australian Standard White to A$200.00 a tonne and its A$5.00 increase in the 1997/98 pool price estimate to A$180.00-A$190.00.
But he said the increases were good news which came amid considerable market volatility and forecasts of lower returns for the coming season, he said.
"There has been a general expectation of price falls this year, resulting from increasing world grain stocks and a seven percent increase in world production," he said.

Record world grain prices in 1996 reflected low stock levels and extreme sensitivity to market developments, but the prospect of another large world harvest in 1997/98 and an increase in world stocks were expected to keep prices under pressure throughout the coming year, he said.
Arney said the industry was currently in a strong position but acknowledged that it had been a difficult year because of the need to reach a conclusion on the restructure of the AWB.

The GCA model blueprint for the future AWB provided the best possible basis for retention of the single desk export monopoly, grower ownership and control, an adequate capital base, commercial flexibility and industry self-determination, he said.
The model is based on A and B class shares and involves creation of separate AWB subsidiaries to conduct wheat pooling and commercial activities under a holding company structure.

Arney said the A$6.7 billion gross value of production for Australia's grains industry was four times that of the fruit industry including wine grapes, twice that of the vegetable industry, 20 percent larger than livestock slaughterings and 20 percent larger than livestock products including milk and wool.
As Australia's largest farm commodity exporter, the grains industry accounted for about one-quarter of the value of total farm exports, he said.
He said that in 1996/97 Australia would export about 74 percent of its grains production, up from 66 percent in 1995/96.

The value of grain exports would be more than six times that of fruit and wine, three times that of dairy products, 40 percent more than meat including sheep and cattle and one-third more than that of wool, including semi-processed skins, he said.
Arney also urged the grains industry to consider a quality assurance programme to guarantee product quality and safety.
This would command a price premium as markets became more quality-conscious and demanding, he said.
